title: The scan before sleep
hook: many people find a slow scan helps them drift off

segments.voice: Yesterday: the jaw, the shoulders and the belly, where the day gets stored. Your line was let the shoulders down.

It's midnight. The lights are off. Your body is tired, but your head is running a meeting: tomorrow's list, the thing you said at lunch, a song you can't shake. You roll over and check the time, which makes it worse. You tell yourself firmly to go to sleep, which makes it much worse. There's a quieter way in. Instead of arguing with your thoughts, give your attention somewhere slow to go: a trip through your own body, from the toes up, one part at a time.
screen: `MIDNIGHT, AND A MEETING IN YOUR HEAD.` → `GO TO SLEEP! (WORSE.)` → `THE SCAN BEFORE SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Sleep has a strange rule: it gets harder the more you try. Sleep researchers call it sleep effort. Straining to fall asleep keeps the brain alert, the opposite of what you want. So the scan before sleep doesn't force sleep. It steps out of the way. Two days ago, the body scan was about noticing, wide awake. At night it changes a little. You lie down and move slowly, feet, ankles, calves, knees, and at each place you add one small invitation: this part can rest now. You're not checking whether it does. You give permission, and move on. It works on two fronts. It gives the busy mind a simple, dull job, like counting sheep with more to feel. And it lets yesterday's muscles, the jaw, the shoulders, the belly, finally let go. If you fall asleep before you reach your knees, that's a success. India has a cousin of this with an old name. In the twentieth century, Swami Satyananda Saraswati shaped a practice he called yoga nidra, yogic sleep: lying down, moving awareness around the body part by part. The name reaches much further back. In the Devi Mahatmya, Yoganidra is the sleep, praised there as the goddess, that holds Vishnu on the cosmic ocean between one age of the world and the next. Two different roots, one simple move: a body visited gently, part by part. And if you're still awake at the top of your head, start again at the toes. Nothing is lost.
screen: `TRYING HARDER DOESN'T WORK.` · `THIS PART CAN REST NOW.` · `A DULL JOB FOR A BUSY MIND.` · `YOGA NIDRA, YOGIC SLEEP.` · then, large: `EVERY PART CAN REST.`

segments.voice: This is a rehearsal for tonight: lie down if you can, or lean back, and let your eyes close. Starting at the feet, say inside, my feet can rest now, then move up: the legs, the hips, the belly soft, the chest and the breath slow, the hands heavy, the shoulders down, the jaw loose, the eyes. Don't check whether it worked; give each part permission and move on.
Yoga nidra. Yogic sleep: a slow trip through the body at bedtime, giving each part permission to rest instead of forcing sleep. Today's word.
Your line: every part can rest. If you drift off halfway, that's the practice working. Day one hundred thirty-four, done.

howItsDone: Many people use a guided body scan or a yoga nidra recording in bed, lying still while attention moves slowly through the body, and some fall asleep before it ends.

original.note: Sanskrit, yoga nidra: yogic sleep. in Hindu stories, Yoganidra is Vishnu's divine sleep; the modern practice is twentieth century.

trapdoor: what you thought: a trick to knock yourself out.
what it means: giving each part of the body permission to rest, instead of forcing sleep.
what a scholar hears: it sidesteps 'sleep effort'; its cousin yoga nidra was shaped by Swami Satyananda Saraswati, borrowing an old name for Vishnu's sleep.
recall: thinking ahead about losses, calmly, once

notes: Swami Satyananda Saraswati's book Yoga Nidra: confirm date (commonly 1976) and that he developed the method from the 1960s.
Yoganidra as the goddess/sleep of Vishnu at the end of an age (Devi Mahatmya ch. 1, Madhu and Kaitabha): confirm framing; a Hindu Keeper may prefer different wording.
'Sleep effort' as a term: confirm (Broomfield & Espie 2005, Glasgow Sleep Effort Scale).
The claim that a scan helps many drift off is framed as what people report, not a proven cure.
